title: Memphis Light, Gas and Water Division v. Craft
lead: Two sets of utility bills confuse homeowners who repeatedly seek an explanation and lose service. Their case asks whether a cutoff notice and nominal complaint channels gave them a usable chance to correct billing errors.

actors.name: Willie S. and Mary Craft
actors.role: Memphis homeowners challenging disputed bills and five utility cutoffs.

actors.name: Memphis Light, Gas and Water Division
actors.role: Municipal utility ultimately controlled by the city.

actors.name: Utility officials and employees
actors.role: Defendants sued in personal and official capacities; petitioners within the Court’s references to the utility.

proceedings: The district court denied class certification and entered judgment for defendants after trial, while recommending a credit and clearer notices.
The Sixth Circuit affirmed denial of class status but held the Crafts’ process unconstitutional.
The Supreme Court affirmed on May 1, 1978, leaving damages and additional unpresented safeguards unresolved.
limits: This account follows the canonical source brief, without a new audit or current-law certification. The $35 credit was not an adjudicated damages award. State action was abandoned as an objection; dismissal of the municipal division itself was unchallenged. The Court did not order free service, award damages, or decide broader procedural demands lacking a cross-petition.

review.basis: Fresh comparison with the complete effective canonical brief; no new independent opinion verification claimed.

sections.title: The Crafts move into a former duplex with two sets of active meters
sections.cue: Why did two bills appear, and what errors were later established?
paragraphs: Willie S. and Mary Craft moved into a former duplex in October 1972. The house contained two gas meters, two electric meters and one water meter. Based on the seller’s information, they believed the second gas and electric meters were inactive. Their provider, Memphis Light, Gas and Water Division, was a municipal division managed by commissioners appointed by the City Council and ultimately controlled by the city, which exempted it from state public-service-commission regulation.

In 1973 the Crafts began receiving separate bills, one addressed to Willie S. Craft and another to Willie C. Craft. Both contained a city service fee. A meter reader explained in October that both sets of meters were operating. A plumber and electrical contractor tried to consolidate them but did not succeed correctly. Separate bills continued through January 1974, and the utility terminated service five times during disputed nonpayment.

Mrs. Craft repeatedly missed work to seek an explanation at the utility’s offices. The district court found her attempts to understand apparent double billing were in good faith, but she received neither a satisfactory explanation nor adequate direction about further recourse. Litigation later revealed improper combination of the accounts in the computer system and overcharges for gas and city service fees. That did not mean every bill from separate working meters duplicated the same consumption.

sources.pinpoint: Meters, disputed bills and repeated terminations; 436 U.S. 3–5 & nn.1–3, 8 n.7, 9 n.8

sections.title: The utility has complaint procedures, but access to them is disputed
sections.cue: What process was nominally available before the Crafts sued?
paragraphs: The utility normally mailed a bill, then a final notice, disconnected electricity, and later disconnected remaining services absent payment or arrangements. Employees could postpone cutoffs for certain explanations. A hardship program permitted half the overdue amount immediately and the balance over three bills. Credit counselors and management nominally handled complaints, with a possible appeal to commissioners.

The final notice warned of the deadline and cutoff. One flyer covering areas with about forty percent of customers offered credit assistance without discussing disputes. Another mentioned disputes, but the record did not establish that the Crafts received it. Their constitutional claim concerned meaningful access to authorized bill reviewers before termination, not simply the existence of an organizational structure somewhere within the utility.

sources.pinpoint: Meters and general procedures; Notice and usable opportunity; 436 U.S. 5–6 n.4, 13–17

sections.title: Trial and appeal separate the personal claim from a proposed class
sections.cue: Why did the case remain live after the bills were clarified and a credit issued?
paragraphs: In February 1974 the Crafts and other customers sued under the federal civil-rights statute, 42 U.S.C. § 1983, seeking declarations, injunctions and actual and punitive damages against the division and its officials and employees. After trial, the district court denied class certification and entered judgment for defendants. It doubted a protected entitlement to continued service during disputed nonpayment and rejected the procedural claim. Nonetheless, it recommended clearer notices and expressed hope for a $35 credit for unnecessary charges and expenses. The credit issued and notices changed.

The Sixth Circuit affirmed denial of class status but held the Crafts’ process constitutionally inadequate. The utility sought Supreme Court review of state action, property and procedural adequacy, then abandoned the state-action objection. The original dismissal of the municipal division under the then-applied § 1983 understanding was unchallenged; references to the utility included individual officials sued personally and officially. The Supreme Court did not retrospectively resolve that separate municipal-liability issue.

With no certified class, jurisdiction depended on the Crafts. They no longer demanded a hearing on an unresolved bill or alleged a presently threatened cutoff, but their damages claim remained. The recommended credit was not an adjudicated award or settlement, and the damages theory was not plainly insubstantial or foreclosed. The Court therefore did not need the capable-of-repetition exception. Whether damages were actually owed remained for initial decision below.

sources.pinpoint: Proceedings, arguments and continuing controversy; 436 U.S. 3–9 & nn.1–8

sections.title: The majority identifies a protected entitlement and an inadequate notice
sections.cue: How did Tennessee law create property without requiring service regardless of payment?
paragraphs: Justice Powell wrote for six Justices. Tennessee law required nondiscriminatory utility service and allowed termination only for good and sufficient cause. It distinguished just, undisputed bills from bona fide disputes: a utility could cut off proper unpaid charges but acted at its peril if contested charges were wrong. Customers paying the undisputed amount retained protection while contesting the rest. An entitlement conditioned on payment of charges actually due remained property even when disputed.

State law supplied the entitlement; federal law determined constitutional protection and adequate procedure. Existing state remedies recognized the interest but did not conclusively establish sufficient process. A for-cause utility relationship differed from entirely at-will service.

The notice conveyed threatened loss but failed adequately to explain how to contest the amount. For customers with varied education, resources and experience, pay-or-lose-service language could render a nominal opportunity ineffective. Customers needed to know where, when and before whom a disputed bill could be considered. The reviewer need not be a corporate officer, only someone empowered to examine and correct the bill. The Court did not demand instruction in every available legal remedy. It acknowledged that the revised notice describing counselors and disputed-bill review might suffice, but that revision was not the adjudicated procedure.

sections.title: An informal internal conference supplies the missing protection
sections.cue: Why were lawsuits and payment under protest insufficient substitutes here?
paragraphs: The customer needed a timely chance to explain an overcharge or charge for unprovided service to an employee able to resolve it. An informal conference could suffice. The Court treated the lower courts as concurrently finding that this opportunity had not been made available to Mrs. Craft. Repeated unsuccessful visits, a later unexplained demand to pay the other account, or eventual discovery of the problem did not establish accessible pre-cutoff review.

Applying Mathews v. Eldridge’s balance of private interest, error risk and additional safeguards against governmental burden, the Court emphasized that gas, water and electricity were necessities. Even brief interruption could threaten health or safety, computer billing presented a meaningful error risk, and an informal meeting before the scheduled cutoff would promote accurate billing without materially delaying collection. The utility retained flexibility in scheduling and structure and could terminate after considering the dispute and finding charges justly due.

A pre-cutoff injunction, later damages or payment followed by a refund suit did not cure this defect. Restoration could not undo an interval without essential services. Modest factual billing disputes seldom justified lawyers and ordinary litigation; injunctions involved procedural barriers and delay. Paying first could be impossible for someone facing unexpected charges, even with an immediate-half-payment plan.

The Court distinguished Ingraham’s school-discipline setting and license revocations following convictions already adjudicated in court. It did not declare damages universally inadequate. The result depended on the serious deprivation, meaningful error risk and modest internal safeguard available here.

sources.pinpoint: Opportunity; Balancing and litigation; 436 U.S. 16–22 & nn.17–28

sections.title: Stevens disagrees with the record assessment and constitutional demand
paragraphs: Justice Stevens dissented with Chief Justice Burger and Justice Rehnquist. He agreed customers had an entitlement while paying undisputed charges, but considered the procedures adequate. Notices displayed deadlines and an information-center number; employees could delay cutoff and refer disputes. In his view Mrs. Craft had reached officials with sufficient authority but had not persuaded them that disputed consumption charges were wrong. Failure to explain access to management did not prove no responsible employee had heard her. He distinguished charges for separate consumption from truly duplicated fees.

Stevens thought notice of the threatened deprivation and time to respond sufficient. Requiring an explicit internal-route explanation was paternalistic and better suited to administrative rulemaking; the utility already processed tens of thousands of complaints. Judicial remedies and damages deterrence provided protection. He criticized reliance on hypothetical health and safety risks rather than harms established in the Crafts’ record and rejected a constitutional requirement of procedures every person could navigate effectively without counsel.

On May 1, 1978, the Court affirmed the Sixth Circuit. It did not award damages or order utilities to provide free service. Nor, absent the Crafts’ cross-petition, did it decide demands for an impartial decisionmaker, fuller rebuttal of records or written decisions. Its distinction of Palmer noted that findings supporting a more extensive remedy there were absent here. The later assigned comparisons with Ingraham, G & G Fire Sprinklers and West Covina remain editorial context, not additional holdings of this decision.

sources.pinpoint: Stevens’s dissent and limits; Assigned scope; 436 U.S. 9 n.8, 12 n.12, 22–30
